                                                  PERIODS OF OKA K3 SURFACES ARE DENSE

                                                              SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO


                                                  Abstract. We give the first known examples of Oka Calabi–Yau




arXiv:2608.24392v2 [math.CV] 17 Sep 2026
                                                  manifolds in any dimension: every smooth hypersurface of multidegree
                                                  (2, . . . , 2) in a product of P1 is Oka. Building on this example, we
                                                  prove that in every local Kuranishi family of K3 surfaces the points
                                                  with Oka fibers form a dense Gδ subset of the base, and the sublocus
                                                  of Oka fibers with vanishing Néron–Severi group is likewise a dense
                                                  Gδ subset. We also obtain projective and nonprojective Oka Kummer
                                                  surfaces and prove an analogous density statement in the Kummer
                                                  period domain. We also prove the existence of Oka Enriques surfaces
                                                  and Oka irreducible hyperkähler fourfolds.




                                                                          1. Introduction
                                              A complex manifold Y is Oka if, for every integer n ≥ 1, every compact
                                           convex set C ⊂ Cn , and every holomorphic map from a neighbourhood of C
                                           to Y , the map can be uniformly approximated on C by entire maps Cn → Y
                                           [10]. This is the convex approximation property (CAP), which Forstnerič
                                           proved to be equivalent to several other classical Oka properties; see also
                                           [11, Ch. 5].
                                              The Oka principle has its roots in the work of Oka and Grauert [27, 15],
                                           while modern Oka theory began with Gromov’s seminal paper [17]. Gromov
                                           placed the theory in the framework of the h-principle and introduced the
                                           notions of elliptic manifolds and dominating sprays. Building on Gromov’s
                                           framework, Forstnerič introduced subellipticity and proved that subelliptic
                                           manifolds are Oka [9]. His work on CAP and its variants led to the modern
                                           formulation of the Oka property [10, 11]. Despite these general criteria,
                                           deciding whether a given complex manifold is Oka remains difficult. A
                                           central problem in Oka theory is to produce new examples of Oka manifolds
                                           and to identify concrete geometric structures that imply the Oka property.
                                              This problem is already subtle for compact complex surfaces. Forstnerič
                                           and Lárusson made a systematic study of their holomorphic flexibility prop-
                                           erties [13]. Among the compact Oka surfaces known from their analysis are
                                           rational surfaces, ruled surfaces over P1 or an elliptic curve, complex tori,
                                           bielliptic surfaces, Kodaira surfaces, minimal Hopf and Enoki surfaces [13,
                                           Th. 4 and § 1]. The Oka problem for K3 surfaces had already been raised
                                           in [12, Problem C] where it is proved that every Kummer K3 surface is
                                           strongly dominable, but it left open whether any Kummer surface, or any
                                           K3 surface, is Oka [13, Cor. 3 and § 1]. More recently, Kummer surfaces
                                                                                    1
2                   SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

and elliptic K3 surfaces were shown to satisfy the weaker Oka-1 property,
while their Oka property remained open [1, Prop. 8.4, Cor. 8.6, and § 8.2].
Prior to the present work, no example of an Oka K3 surface was known.
   We fill this gap and show that Oka K3 surfaces are abundant. By a
local Kuranishi family π : X → B of a K3 surface X0 we mean a proper
holomorphic deformation with central fiber X0 , where B is a smooth complex
manifold, such that the Kodaira–Spencer map T0 B → H1 (X0 , TX0 ) is an
isomorphism. Recall that a Gδ subset of a topological space is a countable
intersection of open subsets.
Theorem A. Let π : X → B be a local Kuranishi family of a K3 surface
with fibers Xb , b ∈ B. Then both
          BOka = {b ∈ B | Xb is Oka}, and {b ∈ BOka | NS(Xb ) = 0}
are dense Gδ subsets of B.
  In other words, for every K3 surface, a Baire-generic member of its local
deformation space is Oka. Here “generic” is understood in the sense of Baire
category, not in the Zariski sense. Since a K3 surface with trivial Néron–
Severi group is nonprojective and contains no curves, we obtain especially
a dense Gδ set of nonprojective, curve-free Oka K3 surfaces in every local
deformation space.
  The density in Theorem A, together with the variety of examples pro-
duced below and in a forthcoming paper of ours, leads us to the following
conjecture.
Conjecture. Every K3 surface is Oka.
  For m ≥ 2, a smooth hypersurface of multidegree (2, . . . , 2) in (P1 )m+1 is
a Calabi–Yau manifold, called a Wehler Calabi–Yau m-fold (see [7]). When
m = 2 it is a K3 surface. The geometric starting point of the proof of
Theorem A is the following explicit families of projective Oka Calabi–Yau
manifolds.
Theorem B (Cor. 3.4). Every Wehler Calabi–Yau manifold is Oka.
    By using Wehler K3 surfaces, we can also prove
Theorem C (Cor. 3.5). Every unnodal Enriques surface is Oka.
    and
Theorem D (Thm. 6.5). There exist irreducible hyperkähler fourfolds which
are Oka.
   We note that in any moduli space of polarized Enriques surfaces, the
unnodal ones form a dense Zariski-open locus. We don’t know whether any
or every nodal Enriques surface is Oka or not.
   Theorem A can also be formulated in Hodge-theoretic terms. For back-
ground on markings, the K3 lattice, and the period domain, see [19]. A
                              OKA K3 SURFACES                                  3

marking of a K3 surface X is an isometry φ : H2 (X, Z) → Λ, where Λ =
3U ⊕2E8 (−1) is the K3 lattice, U has Gram matrix ( 01 10 ), and E8 (−1) is the
negative definite E8 lattice. If ω ∈ H2,0 (X) is a non-zero 2-form, then the pe-
riod is defined to be the oriented positive plane PX = φ(spanR {Re ω, Im ω}).
The K3 period domain D is defined to be the space of oriented two-planes
on which the form of ΛR is positive definite. We denote by NS(X) =
H2 (X, Z) ∩ H1,1 (X) the Néron–Severi lattice. For a marking φ, we have
φ(NS(X)) = Λ ∩ PX⊥ . For a complex two-torus A, we denote by Kum(A) the
minimal resolution of A/{±1}. Such a surface is K3 and is called a Kum-
mer surface. Let A[2] be the subgroup of 2-torsion points. The quotient
A/{±1} has sixteen nodes. If Ea , a ∈ A[2], are the exceptional curves (of
the resolution) on Kum(A), then the lattice
             Kum := H2 (Kum(A), Z) ∩ spanQ {[Ea ] | a ∈ A[2]}
is called the Kummer lattice. It is negative definite of rank 16 and has
discriminant 26 . Its primitive embedding in Λ is unique up to composition
with elements of the orthogonal group O(Λ) [19, Ch. 14, Cor. 3.15]. Fix
such an embedding Kum ⊂ Λ, let L := Kum⊥ , and let DK := {P ∈ D |
P ⊥ Kum}. Then L has signature (3, 3), dimC D = 20, and dimC DK = 4.
Nikulin’s criterion [26, Th. 3] says that a K3 surface is Kummer if and only
if its Néron–Severi lattice contains a primitive copy of Kum. Hence every
period in DK represents a marking of a Kummer surface.
Theorem E. Let O ⊂ D be the set of periods represented by marked K3
surfaces which are Oka, and let OK := O ∩ DK .
    (1) The set O is dense Gδ in D, and so is {P ∈ O | Λ ∩ P ⊥ = 0}.
    (2) The set OK is dense Gδ in DK , and so is {P ∈ OK | Λ∩P ⊥ = Kum}.
In particular, there exist projective and nonprojective Oka Kummer surfaces.
  The construction leading to the theorem also produces a positive-
dimensional family of projective Oka Kummer surfaces. In a forthcoming
paper, we will prove that every projective Kummer surface is Oka. We note
that the density of Oka parameters asserted by Theorem E works on the
period domain which is a Hodge-theoretic parameter space, and it does not
imply density of Oka parameters in a moduli of polarized K3 surfaces.

                          2. Strategy and plan
  In Section 3 we prove Theoerem B. The idea is as follows. Whenever
a Calabi–Yau manifold admits a one-dimensional fibration, or whenever a
hyperkähler manifold admits a Lagrangian fibration, one can use the holo-
morphic volume form or the holomorphic sympletic form to build a holomor-
phic spray. A Wehler Calabi–Yau manifold admits naturally fibrations onto
products of P1 for which the corresponding one-dimensional sprays form a
dominating family. This construction could also work for some other K3
surfaces with two elliptic fibrations, especially those with rich dynamics, see
4                   SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

Cor. 3.8. The method is flexible and could also be adapted to some other
situations. Theorem C about Oka Enriques sufaces is a quick consequence.
However the construction of the hyperkähler example is technically more
involved and is thus postponed to Section 6, though the mechanism of the
construction is the same as those in Section 3.
   In Section 4 we discuss one very special example of K3 surface: the Fermat
quartic. Drawing on classical algebraic geometry of pencils of hyperplane
sections, we show that it is simultaneously a K3 surface of type (2, 2, 2) and
a Kummer surface. Therefore Theorem B implies the existence of an Oka
Kummer surface. Such classical algebro-geometric arguments also play a
crucial rule in the construction of open Oka varieties by the first author [33].
We will also show that the particular needed feature of the Fermat quartic
survives in a positive-dimensional deformation family. This deformation is
crucial for our later application.
   In Section 5 we apply Ratner’s theory to obtain the density assertion
in Theorem A, while the Gδ property is already available by Lárusson’s
work [22, Cor. 8]. Ratner [29] established deep classification theorems for
orbit closures of unipotent flows on homogeneous spaces. Verbitsky [31, 32]
applied this theory to the action of the K3 modular group on the period
domain. In particular Verbitsky asserts that a totally irrational K3 period
has dense orbit in the period domain. Our deformation of the Fermat quartic
constructed in Section 4 provides Oka marked K3 surfaces with such totally
irrational periods.

            3. Holomorphic forms, fibrations and sprays
   Gromov [17] introduced the notion of spray. A spray on a complex man-
ifold X is a holomorphic vector bundle p : E → X and a holomorphic map
s : E → X such that s(0x ) = x. Its vertical differential at 0x is the restric-
tion of ds0x to the fiber direction Ex . A finite set of sprays is dominating if
the images of these vertical differentials span Tx X at every point. A mani-
fold carrying a dominating family is called subelliptic. It is known that every
subelliptic manifold is Oka (see [9] and [11, Cor. 5.6.14]). We say that a
spray s : E → X with bundle projection p : E → X preserves a fibration
f : X → B if f ◦ s = f ◦ p. In this case s(Ex ) is contained in the fiber
f −1 (f (x)) for every x.
3.1. Vertical integration. Let f : X → B be a holomorphic map between
complex manifolds and let π : E → B be a holomorphic vector bundle. A
point of f ∗ E is a pair (x, λ) with λ ∈ Ef (x) .
   We will say that a spray s : f ∗ E → X is additive over B if it preserves f
and if
(3.1)             s(s(x, λ), µ) = s(x, λ + µ),   λ, µ ∈ Ef (x) .
For a local section a of an additive E, we define
(3.2)                       τa (x) := s(x, a(f (x))).
                                 OKA K3 SURFACES                                     5

By (3.1), this is a local biholomorphism with inverse τ−a .
   Assume from now on that A : f ∗ E → TX is a holomorphic morphism of
vector bundles such that df ◦ A = 0. For a local section a of E, we define
its vertical vector field by Va (x) := Ax (a(f (x))).
Lemma 3.1. There is a spray on f ∗ E which preserves f and has vertical
differential A. It is additive if [Va , Vb ] = 0 for all local sections a, b defined
on a common open set. This condition always holds when E has rank one.
Proof. We consider f ∗ E as a complex submanifold of X × E. A vector
(v, η) ∈ Tx X × Tλ E is tangent to f ∗ E if and only if dfx (v) = dπλ (η). Define
locally a vector field on f ∗ E by Ve(x,λ) := (Ax (λ), 0), where 0 is the zero
vector in Tλ E. Since df ◦ A = 0, the local definitions glue to a globally
defined holomorphic vector field Ve on f ∗ E.
   The flow of Ve through (x, λ) remains in the compact set f −1 (f (x)) × {λ}
and exists for every complex time. Its time-one map, composed with the
projection onto X, gives rise to a spray s preserving f . At λ = 0 the vector
field vanishes, and its first variation in the parameter is Ax . Thus the vertical
differential of the spray s is A.
   If the Va commute, then the flow of a sum is the composition of their
flows, and we obtain (3.1). In the rank-one case, two such vector fields have
the form (u ◦ f )V and (v ◦ f )V , where u, v are holomorphic functions on the
base and V is vertical. Since V annihilates both coefficients, their bracket
vanishes.                                                                       □
3.2. Holomorphic symplectic forms. A holomorphic symplectic form is
a closed, everywhere nondegenerate holomorphic 2-form. Now we consider
a holomorphic symplectic manifold X equipped with a such a form σ.
   For a tangent vector v and a differential k-form η, we denote by ιv η the
contraction of η with v, i.e. (ιv η)(v1 , . . . , vk−1 ) = η(v, v1 , . . . , vk−1 ). We
denote the inverse of the contraction v 7→ ιv σ by σ ♯ : TX∗ → TX . For a
subspace W ⊂ Tx X, its symplectic orthogonal is defined as W ⊥ = {v ∈
Tx X | σx (v, w) = 0 for all w ∈ W }. A smooth submanifold Y ⊂ X is called
coisotropic if (Tx Y )⊥ ⊂ Tx Y at every x ∈ Y , and Lagrangian if equality
holds. In particular, smooth hypersurfaces are coisotropic. A fibration on
X is called Lagrangian if its smooth fibers are Lagrangian.
   If f : X → B is a proper surjective holomorphic map between complex
manifolds, and if the smooth fibers of f are coisotropic, then we can define
a morphism of bunldes Af : f ∗ TB∗ → TX by
(3.3)           Af := σ ♯ ◦ df ∗ ,     σx (Af,x (λ), v) = λ(dfx (v)).
Let fj : X → Bj , 1 ≤ j ≤ k, be finitely many maps satisfying the above
hypotheses.
Proposition 3.2. The morphism Af is the vertical differential of an addi-
tive spray on TB∗ . If X is compact and (f1 , . . . , fk ) is an immersion, then
the corresponding sprays form a dominating family, hence X is Oka.
6                    SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

Proof. Over the regular values of f , we have im Af = (ker df )⊥ ⊂ ker df .
The regular locus being dense and open, we have df ◦ Af = 0 everywhere.
   Let a, b be holomorphic 1-forms on an open set U ⊂ B. On f −1 (U ), recall
that we have vector fields Va (x) = Af,x (a(f (x))) and Vb (x) = Af,x (b(f (x))).
By (3.3), we have ιVa σ = f ∗ a and ιVb σ = f ∗ b. Since df (Va ) = df (Vb ) = 0,
for every holomorphic differential form η of positive degree on U we have
ιVa (f ∗ η) = ιVb (f ∗ η) = 0.
   We denote by LV the Lie derivative along a vector field V . By Car-
tan’s formula and dσ = 0, we obtain LVa σ = d(ιVa σ) = f ∗ (da). Moreover,
LVa (f ∗ b) = d(ιVa (f ∗ b)) + ιVa (f ∗ (db)) = 0. We get thus

           ι[Va ,Vb ] σ = LVa (ιVb σ) − ιVb (LVa σ) = −ιVb (f ∗ (da)) = 0.

As σ is nondegenerate, we have [Va , Vb ] = 0. By Lemma 3.1, we obtain the
desired additive spray.
   If the product map is an immersion, its dual differential is surjective. Thus
the images of the dfj∗ span Tx∗ X. By (3.3), the vertical differentials span Tx X
at every point. In other words these sprays form a finite dominating family.
Hence X is subelliptic and therefore Oka by Forstnerič’s theorem [9].           □

3.3. Holomorphic volume forms. Let now X have dimension m ≥ 2
and admit a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic m-form Ω, i.e. a holomorphic
volume form. For a proper holomorphic map f : X → B to a smooth
(m − 1)-fold, define a morphism of bundles Af : f ∗ KB → TX , where KB
denotes the canonical bundle of B, by

For a holomorphic map Φ : X → B1 × · · · × BN to a product of smooth
curves andQ a subset J ⊂ {1, . . . , N } of cardinality m − 1, we denote by
fJ : X → j∈J Bj the composition of Φ with the coordinate projection.

Proposition 3.3. The morphism Af is the vertical differential of an addi-
tive spray on f ∗ KB over X. If X is compact and Φ is an immersion, then
the sprays associated with the fJ form a finite dominating family, hence X
is Oka.

Proof. For ξ ∈ Tf∗(x) B, we obtain from (3.4) that f ∗ ξ ∧ιAf (λ) Ω = f ∗ (ξ ∧λ) =
0. Since the left-hand side is ξ(df (Af (λ)))Ω, we deduce that df ◦ Af = 0.
Thus we can construct a spray preserving f by Lem. 3.1. The additive
property of the spray follows from the rank-one case of Lem. 3.1.
   If X is compact, every fJ is proper. If Φ is also an immersion, the images
of the cotangent lines of the factors span Tx∗ X. Their (m − 1)-fold exterior
products therefore span m−1 Tx∗ X. By (3.4), the vertical differentials span

  Recall that, for m ≥ 2, a Wehler Calabi–Yau m-fold is a smooth hyper-
surface of multidegree (2, . . . , 2) in (P1 )m+1 ; the fact that it is Calabi–Yau
can be seen easily by the adjunction formula (see [7]).
Corollary 3.4. Every Wehler Calabi–Yau manifold is Oka.
Proof. A Calabi–Yau manifold admits a holomorphic volume form. The
inclusion of a Wehler manifold into (P1 )m+1 satisfies the hypotheses of
Prop. 3.3. Remark that when m = 2 the volume form is a symplectic
form and we can also apply Prop. 3.2 to the three projections onto P1 . □

  We say that a complex Enriques surface is unnodal if it contains no (−2)-
curves.
Corollary 3.5. Every unnodal Enriques surface is Oka.
Proof. By [4, Th. 5.1], every unnodal Enriques surface Y has an étale dou-
ble cover X which is a Wehler K3 surface. By Cor. 3.4 X is Oka. We
conclude because the Oka property survives under topological coverings,
see [11, Prop. 5.6.3].                                                  □

3.4. A dynamical criterion. Let X be a complex manifold. For each
index i, let fi : X → Bi be a proper holomorphic map, let Ei → Bi be
a holomorphic vector bundle, and let si : fi∗ Ei → X be an additive spray,
with vertical differential Ai . Define the set
                           (                              )
                                     X
(3.5)               U :=    x∈X|          im(Ai,x ) = Tx X .
                                      i

The set U is open because the spanning condition at one point involves only
finitely many vectors which persist in a neighborhood of that point.
   For a holomorphic section a of Ei over an open subset of Bi , Recall that
we have defined in (3.2) a local biholomorphism τi,a (x) = si (x, a(fi (x))).
Let P be a pseudogroup generated by such local biholomorphisms and the
group Aut(X). The P-orbit of a point x is the set of points obtainable from
x by finite compositions of the generators and their inverses, wherever these
compositions are defined.
   Following [21], for a holomorphic map h : S → X, we will say that a spray
over h with parameter space Cn is a holomorphic map H : S × Cn → X
satisfying H(s, 0) = h(s) for every s ∈ S. We call dt H(s, 0) : Cn → Th(s) X
its parameter differential.
Proposition 3.6. If every P-orbit intersects U , then X is Oka.
Proof. By a theorem of Kusakabe [21, Cor. 4.1], it suffices to prove that,
for every holomorphic map h : S → X from a Stein manifold S and every
s0 ∈ S, there are finitely many sprays over h whose parameter differentials
at s0 span Th(s0 ) X.

Corollary 3.7. Let π : X → P1 × P1 be the double cover branched over a
smooth curve of bidegree (4, 4). The surface X is an Oka K3 surface.
Proof. The double cover of P1 ×P1 branched over a smooth curve of bidegree
(4, 4) is a K3 surface, by a quick application of the adjunction formula (see
[30, Th. 2.2]). We will fix a holomorphic symplectic form on X.
   Let fi = pri ◦π, where pri : P1 × P1 → P1 is the i-th projection. By
Prop. 3.2 we obtain additive sprays si : fi∗ TP∗1 → X with vertical differentials
Ai . Let P be the pseudogroup defined above with respect to these sprays.
   By (3.3), the images of A1,x and A2,x span Tx X exactly when dπx is
invertible. Let R ⊂ X be the ramification curve of π. Thus the set U
defined in (3.5) is X \ R.
   Fix x ∈ R. As R is smooth, in suitable local coordinates centered at x and
π(x), we have π(z, w) = (z, w2 ) and R = {w = 0}. Hence ker(dπx ) ∩ Tx R =
{0}. Let i ∈ {1, 2} such that dfi,x ̸= 0. Remark that im(Ai,x ) = ker(dfi,x ) =
ker(dπx ). For a local holomorphic one-form a on P1 with a(fi (x)) ̸= 0, we
have
                     d                               
                           τi,ta (x) = Ai,x a(fi (x)) ∈/ Tx R.
                    dt t=0
As a consequence, τi,ta (x) ∈ U for every sufficiently small t ̸= 0. Thus every
P-orbit meets U , and we conclude by Prop. 3.6.                                □
   Let X be a projective K3 surface. We say that Aut(X) is non-elementary
if its action on GL(H2 (X, Z)) contains a nonabelian free subgroup. An
automorphism g ∈ Aut(X) is called parabolic if it has infinite order and
preserves a genus-one fibration.
Corollary 3.8. Assume that X is a K3 surface such that Aut(X) is non-
elementary, contains a parabolic automorphism, and preserves no nonempty
proper algebraic subset of X. Then X is Oka.
Proof. As Aut(X) is non-elementary, there are two parabolic automorphisms
whose invariant genus-one fibrations f1 , f2 : X → P1 are distinct (see [5]).
We will fix a holomorphic symplectic form σ on X. By Prop. 3.2, we have
additive sprays si : fi∗ TP∗1 → X with vertical differentials Ai . Let P be the
pseudogroup considered above generated by Aut(X) and the local biholo-
morphisms defined by the sprays.
  The set U defined in (3.5) satisfies
(3.10)           U = {x ∈ X | ker(df1,x ) ∩ ker(df2,x ) = {0}} .
10                   SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

As the morphism (f1 , f2 ) : X → P1 ×P1 is generically finite, U is a nonempty
Zariski-open subset of X.
   For every x ∈ X, the Zariski closure of the orbit Aut(X) · x is a nonempty
Aut(X)-invariant algebraic subset. By hypothesis it is X, so the orbit in-
tersects U . We conclude by Prop. 3.6.                                      □
Remark 3.9. Cor. 3.8 is one of the major inspiration/motivation for our
work. We refer to [6] for examples of K3 surfaces satisfying the hypothesis
of Cor. 3.8.

             4. The Fermat quartic and Kummer surfaces
   In this section we will show that many Kummer surfaces are Oka, in-
cluding some examples with totally irrational period. In the first subsection
we study the Fermat quartic and in the second subsection we construct one
deformation family of it.
4.1. A (2, 2, 2) model. Choose a root of unity ζ ∈ C with i = ζ 2 . Consider
the Fermat quartic in P3 defined in homogeneous coordinates by x40 + x41 +
x42 + x43 = 0. It is a K3 surface, see [19, § 1.1.3]. Via the linear change of
coordinates x0 = ζX, x1 = Y , x2 = ζZ, x3 = W , it is isomorphic to
                      Q = {Y 4 + W 4 = X 4 + Z 4 } ⊂ P3 .
It contains the three pairwise disjoint lines
     L1 = {X = Y, Z = W }, L2 = {X = iY, Z = −W }, L3 = {X = −Y, Z = iW }.
   Let H denote the hyperplane class on Q. For each j, every plane through
Lj cuts Q in a divisor of the form Lj + C, where C is a plane cubic. As the
plane varies, these cubics form a pencil of divisors of class H − Lj where H
denotes the hyperplane class.
Lemma 4.1. For each j = 1, 2, 3, the cubics cut out on Q by the planes
through Lj form a base-point-free pencil whose general member is a smooth
genus-one curve.
Proof. Fix j and let l0 , l1 be two independent linear equations defining Lj .
Since Lj ⊂ Q, the defining quartic equation of Q can be written as l0 A +
l1 B = 0 where A and B are some cubic forms.
   For [a : b] ∈ P1 , let P[a:b] be the plane al0 + bl1 = 0. Its intersection with
Q is the union of Lj and the residual cubic
                    C[a:b] = {al0 + bl1 = 0, bA − aB = 0}.
  It is clear that the pencil has no base point outside Lj . If p ∈ Lj were a
base point, then p ∈ C[a:b] for every [a : b] ∈ P1 , so bA(p) − aB(p) = 0 for
every [a : b]. Consequently A(p) = B(p) = 0. Since l0 (p) = l1 (p) = 0, we
would then have
                  d(l0 A + l1 B)p = A(p) dl0p + B(p) dl1p = 0,
contrary to the smoothness of Q.
                              OKA K3 SURFACES                                 11

  Thus the pencil is base-point-free. By Bertini’s theorem, its general mem-
ber is smooth. Each member is a plane cubic, so every smooth member has
genus one.                                                                □
  For j = 1, 2, 3, let πj : Q → P1 be the morphism defined by the pencil of
Lemma 4.1, and let Fj denote its fiber divisor class. Since a plane through
Lj cuts Q in Lj and a fiber of πj , we have the equality Fj = H − Lj between
divisor classes on Q. As the intersection numbers satisfy H 2 = 4, HLj = 1,
and as the lines Lj are pairwise disjoint, we obtain Fj Fk = 2 for j ̸= k.
Proposition 4.2. The morphism Φ : Q → (P1 )3 induced by the three pencils
constructed above is an isomorphism onto a smooth hypersurface of multi-
degree (2, 2, 2).
Proof. We first prove that Φ is a finite morphism. If an irreducible curve
C ⊂ Q were contracted by all three πj , then for each j it would lie in a
plane through Lj . As the first two such planes inteserct in one line, the
curve C would itself be a line on Q. Remark that by construction this line
would meet each Lj because it shares a plane with each of them. A direct
computation with the explicit equations of the three lines Lj shows that no
such line would exist.
   We next prove that Φ is birational onto its image, i.e. has degree one.
We prove this by showing that a general value has only one preimage. At
p = [1 : 0 : 0 : 1] ∈ Q, the three planes corresponding to the fibers of
π1 , π2 , π3 through p have equations
  X − Y + Z − W = 0,       X − iY − Z − W = 0,        X + Y − iZ − W = 0.
The determinant of their coefficients in X, Y, Z is 2, so these three planes
intersect in the single point p. The same is true for triples of fiber planes
parametrized by a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the image of Φ. In other
words a general fiber of Φ consists of one point.
   Denote Y = Φ(Q). Since Φ is a finite morphism, Y is an integral sur-
face in (P1 )3 . As (P1 )3 is smooth, the Weil divisor Y is Cartier (see [18,
Prop. 2.6.11]). Let Hj denote the class on (P1 )3 of the pullback line bundle
of OP1 (1) from the j-th factor of (P1 )3 . Then [Y ] = aH1 + bH2 + cH3 where
(a, b, c) is the multidegree of Y . Since Φ∗ Hj = Fj and Φ∗ [Q] = [Y ], we
obtain the intersection numbers a = F2 F3 , b = F1 F3 , and c = F1 F2 by the
projection formula (see [14, Prop. 2.3(c)]). Hence a = b = c = 2.
   As Y is a Cartier divisor in (P1 )3 , it is Cohen—Macaulay, i.e. locally
complete intersection (see [18, Th. II.8.21, Prop. II.8.23]). By the adjunction
formula (see [18, Th. 7.11]), the dualizing sheaf of Y is trivial. Since the
dualizing sheaf of the smooth surface Q is simply its canonical bundle, it
is also trivial. Hence the conductor of the finite morphism Φ : Q → Y is
trivial by [28, Prop. 2.9] (see also [18, Ex. III.7.2]). This means that Φ is an
isomorphism.                                                                   □
Corollary 4.3. The Fermat quartic is an Oka Kummer surface.
12                   SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

Proof. By Proposition 4.2 and Corollary 3.4, the Fermat quartic is Oka. It
is a Kummer surface by Mizukami’s theorem, see [20, App. Th. A.1].      □
4.2. Deformations preserving the three pencils. Recall that Λ is the
K3 lattice from the introduction. Again we refer to [19] for background on
lattices and cohomological aspects of K3 surfaces. In this subsection we will
fix a marking H2 (Q, Z) → Λ which sends its Kummer sublattice to the fixed
primitive sublattice Kum ⊂ Λ. Via this marking, we also regard the fiber
classes F1 , F2 , F3 as elements of Λ. Let ΛQ ⊂ Λ be the smallest primitive
sublattice containing Kum, F1 , F2 , F3 .
   By Prop. 4.2, the class F1 + F2 + F3 is the pullback of O(P1 )3 (1, 1, 1), thus
ample. The Hodge index theorem then implies that ΛQ is nondegenerate of
signature (1, rk ΛQ − 1). Since rk Kum = 16, we have rk ΛQ ≤ 19. Hence
the period domain
(4.1)                      DQ = {P ∈ D | P ⊥ ΛQ }
is contained in the Kummer period domain DK and has complex dimension
(4.2)                           20 − rk ΛQ ≥ 1.
   The following proposition performs a deformation of Prop. 4.2. It is the
key geometric input for the dynamical machinery that we investigate later
in Section 5.
Proposition 4.4. A nonempty open subset of DQ parametrizes Kummer
surfaces which are smooth hypersurfaces of multidegree (2, 2, 2) in (P1 )3 .
All these surfaces are Oka.
Proof. Let p : X → T be a local Kuranishi family of Q over a simply
connected base T , with central point 0 ∈ T . Our fixed marking H2 (Q, Z) →
Λ extends to a trivialization of R2 p∗ Z, i.e. it induces markings on nearby
fibers. The induced local period map per : T → D is a local biholomorphism
by the local Torelli theorem (see [19, Ch. 6,7]).
    Let B := per−1 (DQ ). Up to shrinking T , we can and will assume that
the period map sends B biholomorphically to a neighborhood of the period
of Q in DQ . By definition (4.1) of DQ , every class in ΛQ , and in particular
each Fi , is orthogonal to the period, thus of type (1, 1) on every fiber over
B. Therefore they are classes of line bundles. The line bundles OQ (Fi ) thus
extend to line bundles Li on X (see [19, Ch. 6, §2.4] for the arguments in
this paragraph).
    We have OQ (Fi ) ≃ πi∗ OP1 (1) for the fibration πi : Q → P1 , so
h (Q, OQ (Fi )) = 2. Moreover, h2 (Q, OQ (Fi )) = h0 (Q, OQ (−Fi )) = 0
  0

by Serre duality (see [2, § I.5]). Since the self-intersection Fi2 = 0 vanishes
because Fi is a fiber class, we get χ(Q, OQ (Fi )) = 2 by the Riemann–Roch
theorem (see [2, § I.5]). Therefore h1 (Q, OQ (Fi )) = 0.
    For b ∈ B, let Xb = p−1 (b) and Li,b = Li |Xb . Since h1 (Q, OQ (Fi )) =
h2 (Q, OQ (Fi )) = 0, by using the semicontinuity theorem (see [16, § 7,
Satz 3]) we can and will assume, up to shrinking B, that h1 (Xb , Li,b ) =
                               OKA K3 SURFACES                                 13

h2 (Xb , Li,b ) = 0 for every b ∈ B. The class of Li,b has self-intersection 0
by definition, so the Riemann–Roch theorem on the K3 surface Xb implies
χ(Xb , Li,b ) = 2. Hence h0 (Xb , Li,b ) = 2 for every b ∈ B. By Grauert’s
theorem [16, § 7, Satz 5], a basis of H0 (Q, OQ (Fi )) extends to two sections
of Li whose restrictions form a basis of H0 (Xb , Li |Xb ) for every b ∈ B. As
these two sections have no common zero on Q, up to shrinking B we can
and will assume that they have no common zero on any fiber. Therefore, by
taking ratios of the two sections we obtain morphisms πi,b : Xb → P1 which
deform the three initial fibrations πi .
   The product Φb = (π1,b , π2,b , π3,b ) : Xb → (P1 )3 is an embedding for b = 0
by Prop. 4.2. Since being an embedding is an open property, up to shrinking
again B we assert that every Φb is an embedding. Its image is a smooth
hypersurface which has necessarily multidegree (2, 2, 2) (see the argument
in Prop. 4.2). Thus every Xb is Oka by Cor. 3.4.
   Finally, remark that by construction Kum is primitive in the Néron–
Severi group NS(Xb ) of every fiber Xb . By Nikulin’s criterion [26, Th. 3] we
conclude that every Xb is a Kummer surface.                                    □
Proposition 4.5. There is a marked Oka Kummer surface with period Pirr ∈
DK such that Pirr ∩ ΛQ = {0}.
Proof. Let B ⊂ DQ be the nonempty open subset provided by Prop. 4.4. For
a nonzero vector v ∈ ΛQ , consider the locus of periods P ∈ DQ containing v.
This locus is empty unless v ∈ ((ΛQ )R )⊥ and v 2 > 0. When it is nonempty,
the positive definite oriented two-planes containing the positive line Rv are
parametrized by positive lines in v ⊥ ∩((ΛQ )R )⊥ . They therefore form a closed
real submanifold of dimension 20 − rk ΛQ , whereas DQ has real dimension
2(20 − rk ΛQ ). By (4.2) this locus is nowhere dense.
   There are only countably many nonzero vectors in ΛQ . Since B is a Baire
space, it contains a period Pirr which contains none of the above loci. In
other words we can find a period satisfying Pirr ∩ ΛQ = {0}.                   □

         5. Period domain and ergodic complex structure
   Let O(Λ) be the isometry group of the K3 lattice Λ and let Γ ⊂ O(Λ) be
a finite-index subgroup preserving D. By Verbitsky’s theorem [32, Th. 2.5]
which is an application of Ratner’s theory [29], the lattice Pirr constructed
in Prop. 4.5 has dense orbit in the period domain:
(5.1)                             Γ · Pirr = D.
Every point of the orbit Γ · Pirr is the period of a marking of the same Oka
surface.
   We need a similar density statement inside the Kummer period domain.
Let L = Kum⊥ ⊂ Λ and let ΓKum ⊂ O(Λ) be the subgroup of O(L) acting
trivially on Kum. We assert that the image of ΓKum in O(L) has finite in-
dex. Indeed, since Kum and L are primitive orthogonal complements in the
unimodular lattice Λ, we have Kum ⊕L ⊂ Λ ⊂ Kum∨ ⊕L∨ where Kum∨ , L∨
14                  SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

denote the dual lattices. If g ∈ O(L) acts trivially on the discriminant group
L∨ /L, then g(y) − y ∈ L for every y ∈ L∨ , so idKum ⊕g preserves Λ. Thus
the image of ΓKum contains ker(O(L) → O(L∨ /L)), which has finite index.
  Let Γ+Kum be the subgroup of ΓKum preserving DK . Its image has finite
index in the subgroup of O(L) preserving DK . Since L has signature (3, 3)
and Pirr ∩ LQ = {0}, Verbitsky’s theorem [32, Th. 2.5] still can be applied,
and we obtain
(5.2)                        Γ+
                              Kum · Pirr = DK .
Every point of this orbit is again the period of a marking of the same Oka
Kummer surface.
Proof of Theorem E. By (5.1), the set O is dense in the period domain D.
We claim that it is also Gδ . By the local Torelli theorem [19, Ch. 6,7] ev-
ery point of D has a neighborhood biholomorphic to the base of a marked
Kuranishi family. Two marked K3 surfaces with the same period have bi-
holomorphic underlying surfaces by the global Torelli theorem [19, Ch. 7,
Th. 5.3]. Thus, the intersection of O with such a neighborhood coincides
with the Oka locus of the corresponding Kuranishi family. This locus is Gδ
by Lárusson’s theorem [22, Cor. 8]. Hence O is locally Gδ in the period
domain, and therefore Gδ by Lemma 5.1 below.
   For every nonzero h ∈ Λ, the locus {P ∈ D | P ⊥ h} is a closed
codimension-one analytic subset. Consequently the locus {P ∈ D | Λ∩P ⊥ =
0} is a dense Gδ subset of D. Its intersection with O is therefore again a
dense Gδ subset because D is a Baire space. For every period in this inter-
section the corresponding K3 surface is nonprojective and contains no curve
because its Néron–Severi group vanishes.
   By (5.2), OK is dense in DK , and it is Gδ because OK = O ∩ DK .
The same argument as above shows that periods with Néron–Severi lattice
exactly equal to Kum form a dense Gδ in DK . Indeed, if h ∈ Λ\Kum, then its
projection to LQ is nonzero because Kum is primitive. Hence the condition
P ⊥ h defines a closed hypersurface in DK . Thus the Oka periods with
Néron–Severi lattice exactly equal to Kum form a dense Gδ in DK . Since
Kum is negative definite, the corresponding K3 surfaces are nonprojective
by the Hodge index theorem.                                               □
Lemma 5.1. Let M be a second-countable metrizable space and let A ⊂ M
be a subset. If A is locally Gδ , then it is Gδ .
Proof. The metrizability ensures that every open subset of M is Fσ . Con-
sider a countable open cover (Uj ) of M such that Uj \ A is Fσ in Uj . Every
subset closed in Uj has the form Uj ∩F with F closed in M , hence is Fσ in M
because Uj is. Thus each Uj \A is Fσ in M , and so is M \A = j (Uj \A). □
                                                             S

Proof of Theorem A. Choose a marking of the local Kuranishi family and
let per : B → D be its period map. By the local Torelli theorem, per is a
local biholomorphism.
                               OKA K3 SURFACES                                 15

   Let V ⊂ B be a nonempty open subset. Then per(V ) is open in D. By
Theorem E, it contains a period represented by an Oka K3 surface. If b ∈ V
has this period, then the corresponding K3 fiber Xb is biholomorphic to that
surface by the global Torelli theorem. Therefore V ∩ BOka ̸= ∅. Since V was
arbitrary, BOka is dense in B. It is Gδ by Lárusson’s theorem [22, Cor. 8].
   Similarly, Theorem E implies that every per(V ) contains an Oka period P
satisfying Λ ∩ P ⊥ = 0. Since φb (NS(Xb )) = Λ ∩ per(b)⊥ , the corresponding
fiber Xb is Oka and satisfies NS(Xb ) = 0. Thus these parameters are also
dense in B. Moreover, the locus where NS(Xb ) = 0 is the inverse image
under per of {P ∈ D | Λ ∩ P ⊥ = 0}, which is Gδ by the proof of Theorem E.
Its intersection with BOka is therefore Gδ .                              □

                   6. An Oka hyperkähler fourfold
   An irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifold is a simply connected
compact Kähler manifold whose space of holomorphic 2-forms is generated
by a symplectic form. Such a manifold is also called an irreducible hyperkäh-
ler manifold. We say that it is of K3[n] -type if it is deformation equivalent
to the Hilbert scheme of length-n subschemes of a K3 surface. For an ir-
reducible hyperkähler manifold there is a quadratic form, called Beauville–
Bogomolov–Fujiki form, on the second integral cohomology (see [3]). In
this section, we only consider hyperkähler fourfolds,     and denote by q the
Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form normalized by α4 = 3q(α)2 .
                                                    R


6.1. Construction. Let S ⊂ (P1 )3 be a Wehler K3 surface, i.e. a smooth
(2, 2, 2) hypersurface. Its coordinate projections pi : S → P1 , for i = 1, 2, 3,
are genus-one fibrations. Let Fi = c1 (p∗i OP1 (1)) be their fiber cohomology
classes. Let X0 = S [2] be the Hilbert scheme of length-two subschemes
of S; it is a hyperkähler variety. Each pi induces a Lagrangian fibration
fi0 : X0 → Sym2 (P1 ) ≃ P2 where Sym2 denotes the symmetric product. A
general fiber of fi0 is a product of two genus-one curves.
    Let E ⊂ X0 be the exceptional divisor of the natural morphism X0 =
S [2] → Sym2 (S), i.e. E parametrizes nonreduced length-two subschemes of
S. By [3, § 6], there is an orthogonal decomposition
(6.1)                        H2 (X0 , Z) ≃ Ω ⊕ Zδ
where 2δ = [E], q(δ) = −2, and q|Ω coincides with the intersection form on
S. Since Ω has rank 22, the second Betti number of X0 is b2 (X0 ) = 23. Via
the decomposition (6.1), the class Fi ∈ Ω corresponds exactly to the fiber
class c1 ((fi0 )∗ OP2 (1)). In the sequel we will denote both classes by Fi .
   Consider the sublattice N := ZF1 + ZF2 + ZF3 . As Fi2 = 0 and Fi · Fj = 2
for i ̸= j, the intersection matrix on N is
                                       
                     3          0 2 2
(6.2)       q(Fi , Fj ) i,j=1 = 2 0 2 ,     so N ≃ U (2) ⊕ ⟨−4⟩,
                                 2 2 0
16                     SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

where U (2) has Gram matrix ( 02 20 ), and ⟨−4⟩ has a generator of square
−4. Here the orthogonal decomposition in (6.2) is compatible to the basis
F1 , F2 , F3 − F1 − F2 . In particular, N has signature (1, 2). By Lefschetz
Theorem the restriction H2 ((P1 )3 , Z/pZ) → H2 (S, Z/pZ) is injective for ev-
ery prime number p. Therefore N is a primitive sublattice in Ω, and hence
in H2 (X0 , Z).
   By [23, § 6.2], there exist a local Kuranishi family of the pair
(X0 , (fi0 )∗ OP2 (1)), i.e. a smooth proper holomorphic family π : X → T
of K3[2] -type fourfolds over a small contractible base, with π −1 (0) = X0 ,
and line bundles Li extending (fi0 )∗ OP2 (1). The fibers have markings
H2 (Xt , Z) ≃ Ω ⊕ Zδ so that c1 (Li |Xt ) = Fi . The period map sends T
biholomorphically to an open neighborhood of H2,0 (X0 ) in the period
domain
           n                                                                     o
(6.3)        [w] ∈ P(H2 (X0 , C)) | q(w) = 0, q(w, w) > 0, q(w, Fi ) = 0 .
As N has rank three, we have dim T = 23 − 3 − 2 = 18.
Lemma 6.1. For t sufficiently close to 0, the line bundles Li |Xt are glob-
ally generated and have three global sections. Their linear systems define
Lagrangian fibrations onto P2 , and the product of these three fibrations has
differential of rank at least two everywhere.
Proof. By Matsushita’s theorem [24, Th. 1.2 and Cor. 1.3], the complete
linear systems of Li |Xt define holomorphic families of Lagrangian fibrations
fit : Xt → P2 extending fi0 , for t near 0. In particular Li |Xt is globally
generated and has three global sections.
   Consider a point ξ ∈ X0 \ E representing two distinct points x, y ∈ S.
For u near x, we have fi0 ({u, y}) = pi (u) + pi (y) ∈ Sym2 (P1 ). Note
that each map b 7→ b + pi (y) embeds P1 into Sym2 (P1 ) as a line.
Since (p1 , p2 , p3 ) : S → (P1 )3 is an embedding, we deduce that u 7→
(f10 ({u, y}), f20 ({u, y}), f30 ({u, y})) is an immersion. Hence d(f10 , f20 , f30 )ξ has
rank at least two.
   Now we study what happens on E. Let ρ : E → S be the natural
projection. For ξ ∈ E, we have fi0 (ξ) = 2pi (ρ(ξ)). As ρ is a submersion,
(p1 , p2 , p3 ) is an embedding, and b 7→ 2b embeds P1 into Sym2 (P1 ) as a conic,
we deduce that the rank of d(f10 , f20 , f30 ) on E is exactly two.
   Thus the product differential has rank at least two everywhere on X0 .
The same holds for d(f1t , f2t , f3t ) for t sufficiently close to 0.                   □
   For every class α ∈ Ω \ N , the equation q(w, α) = 0 defines a proper
closed analytic subset of T . We may choose t arbitrarily close to 0, satisfying
Lemma 6.1 and avoiding all these countably many subsets. Let X := Xt .
Then
(6.4)                                NS(X) = N.
Let fi : X → P2 be the Lagrangian fibrations defined by the complete linear
systems of Li |X , and fix a holomorphic symplectic form σ on X.
                              OKA K3 SURFACES                                17

Lemma 6.2. The hyperkähler fourfold X is projective. Its positive cone is
its Kähler cone. The class F1 + F2 is ample while (f1 , f2 ) : X → (P2 )2 is a
finite morphism.
Proof. The positive cone of X is the component of {β ∈ H1,1 (X, R) | q(β) >
0} containing the Kähler classes. As every element of N has a square di-
visible by four, there is no integral (1, 1)-class on X of square −2 or −10
by (6.4). Then by [25, Prop. 2.12], we deduce that the Kähler cone equals
the positive cone.
   The class F1 + F2 belongs to the positive cone and is a Kähler class.
By Kodaira’s embedding theorem, it is ample and X is projective. Since
a positive-dimensional fiber of (f1 , f2 ) would contain a curve on which the
corresponding ample line bundle has degree zero, the map (f1 , f2 ) : X →
P2 × P2 is finite.                                                         □

6.2. Automorphisms. Let NR := N ⊗Z R, and let O+ (N ) be the group
of integral isometries preserving the component of {β ∈ NR | q(β) > 0}
containing F1 + F2 . Denote by N ∨ the dual lattice {u ∈ N ⊗Z Q | q(u, N ) ⊂
Z}. The discriminant group N ∨ /N is finite, equipped with a quadratic form
[u] 7→ q(u) mod 2Z. We denote its isometry group by O(N ∨ /N ), and the
real algebraic group of determinant-one isometries of NR by SO(NR , q).
   Let N ⊥ be the orthogonal complement of N in H2 (X, Z), and let G :=
{g ∈ Aut(X) | g ∗ |N ⊥ = id}. As the symplectic class satisfies σ ∈ N ⊥ ⊗ C,
every element of G preserves σ.
Lemma 6.3. The image of G in O(N ) contains the kernel of O+ (N ) →
O(N ∨ /N ). Every finite-index subgroup of G acts irreducibly on NR .
Proof. Let γ ∈ ker(O+ (N ) → O(N ∨ /N )). Extend γ to a rational isometry
γe of H2 (X, Q) by using the identity on N ⊥ ⊗ Q. For α ∈ Ω, we denote by
αN its orthogonal projection to N ⊗ Q. Then αN ∈ N ∨ , so γe (α) − α =
γ(αN ) − αN ∈ N . Hence γe (Ω) = Ω. Since γe fixes the class δ (defined in
(6.1)), it defines an integral isometry of H2 (X, Z).
   Note that γe fixes σ and preserves the positive cone. Since Ω is unimodular
and q(δ) = −2, the discriminant group of H2 (X, Z) is Z/2Z, generated by
the class of δ/2. We remak that γe acts trivially on the discriminant group of
H2 (X, Z). By [23, Def. 1.1 and Lem. 9.2], γe is a parallel-transport operator.
Recall that by Lem. 6.2 the Kähler cone equals the positive cone. Therefore
we can apply the Global Torelli Theorem [23, Th. 1.3] to find g ∈ G such
that g ∗ = γe .
   Recall that F1 , F2 , (F3 − F1 − F2 ) is a basis of N . We will think of an
element xF1 + yF2 + z(F3 − F1 − F2 ) ∈ N as a symmetric matrix M = ( xz yz ).
Then q(M ) = 4 det M , and F1 + F2 corresponds to the identity matrix.
Hence the action M 7→ AM At defines a homomorphism SL2 (Z) → O+ (N ).
   Let H ⊂ G be a subgroup of finite index. Then the image of H has finite
index in O+ (N ). Its inverse image Γ ⊂ SL2 (Z) therefore has finite index and
18                    SONG-YAN XIE AND SHENGYUAN ZHAO

is Zariski-dense in SL2 (R). Since the representation of SL2 (R) on symmetric
matrices is irreducible, we conclude that H acts irreducibly on NR .       □

6.3. Invariant surfaces. For an irreducible subvariety Z ⊂ X, we denote
by Zreg its smooth locus, and define StabG (Z) := {g ∈ G | g(Z) = Z}.
Lemma 6.4. If an irreducible surface Z ⊂ X has finite orbit under G, then
σ|Zreg = 0.

Proof. Let µ : Ze → X be the minimal resolution of singularities (see [2,
Th. III.6.2]). The action of StabG (Z) lifts to Ze by uniqueness of the res-
olution. Note that StabG (Z) has finite index in G because Z has finite
orbit.
   The map β 7→ Z β 2 defines a quadratic form on NR which is invari-
                   R

ant under StabG (Z). By representation-irreducibility of StabG (Z) from
Lemma 6.3, there exists c > 0 such that
                Z                   Z
(6.5)                µ∗ β µ ∗ γ =       βγ = c q(β, γ),   β, γ ∈ NR .
                 Z
                 e                  Z

   Suppose now for contradiction that µ∗ σ ̸= 0. Then the kernel of µ∗ :
H (X, Q) → H2 (Z,
 2                e Q) is a rational Hodge substructure without (2, 0)-part
or (0, 2)-part because H2,0 (X) = Cσ. By the Lefschetz (1, 1)-theorem, it
is contained in NS(X) ⊗ Q = N ⊗ Q. If β is in this kernel, then by (6.5)
q(β, γ) = 0 for every γ ∈ N ⊗ Q. As q is nondegenerate on N , we have
β = 0. Thus µ∗ is injective.
   Let R be the zero divisor of µ∗ σ. Since G preserves σ, the divisor R is
invariant under StabG (Z). By Lemma 6.3, the invariant linear functional
β 7→ R · µ∗ β vanishes on NR . For an ample class β, the degree of µ∗ β
on a curve is positive unless the curve is contracted by µ. Therefore every
component of R is contracted by µ.
   For every m ≥ 1 and nonzero s ∈ H0 (Z,e mK ), the poles of s/(µ∗ σ)m are
                                               Ze
supported on R. Being a rational function on Z ν , s/(µ∗ σ)m has no poles in
codimension one. It is thus constant. Therefore h0 (Z,e mK ) = 1 for every
                                                            Ze
m ≥ 1. By the classification of projective surfaces [2], there is a birational
morphism ρ : Ze → Z0 where Z0 is K3 or abelian. Hence the form µ∗ σ
descends to a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic 2-form on Z0 . This implies
that every ρ-exceptional curve occurs in R, thus is contracted by µ. We
then obtain
(6.6)                     µ∗ H2 (X, Q) ⊂ ρ∗ H2 (Z0 , Q).
By the injectivity of µ∗ and (6.6), we deduce 23 = b2 (X) ≤ b2 (Z0 ) ≤ 22, a
contradiction.                                                            □

6.4. The Oka property. We will use the terminology of Section 3. By
Prop. 3.2, each fi induces an additive spray si : fi∗ TP∗2 → X with vertical
                                 OKA K3 SURFACES                                19

differential Ai = σ ♯ ◦ dfi∗ . Let P be the pseudogroup generated by G and
the local biholomorphisms induced these three sprays, as in § 3.4. Define
                          n                                   o
(6.7)               D := x ∈ X | ∩3i=1 ker(dfi,x ) ̸= {0} .

Theorem 6.5. The projective hyperkähler fourfold X is Oka.
Proof. The set D is algebraic. Since (f1 , f2 ) is finite by Lem. 6.2, its differ-
ential has rank four on a nonempty Zariski-open subset, so D ̸= X. The
locus defined in (3.5) is U = X \ D.
   Suppose now for contradiction that a P-orbit O is contained in D. Let
         Zar
W := O . Then W ⊂ D is a G-invariant algebraic subset.
   Let us fix i ∈ {1, 2, 3}, a Zariski-open set V ⊂ P2 , and an algebraic one-
form a on V . On fi−1 (V ), recall that in Section 3 we defined the vector field
Vi,a (x) = Ai,x (a(fi (x))). As σ and fi are algebraic, Vi,a is algebraic. For
a regular local function φ vanishing on W and a point x ∈ O where φ is
defined, we have
                                 d                        
                 Vi,a (φ)(x) =          φ si x, t a(fi (x)) = 0
                                 dt t=0
because the local biholomorphisms in P preserve O. By Zariski density, the
local regular function Vi,a (φ) vanishes on W wherever it is defined. Let Z
be an irreducible component of W . Then Vi,a is tangent to Z at its smooth
points outside the intersection locus with other components of W . The
above arguments show that, at a general point x ∈ Zreg , we have
                     Ai,x Tf∗i (x) P2 ⊆ Tx Z,
                                   
(6.8)                                             i = 1, 2, 3.
   If dim Z = 0, then Ai,x = 0 for every i by (6.8). By (3.3), we would have
dfi,x = 0 for every i, contradiction to Lemma 6.1.
   If dim Z = 3, then [Z] ∈ N would be fixed by StabG (Z) which is a finite-
index subgroup of G because G permutes the components of W . This would
contradict Lem. 6.3.          R
   If dim Z = 1, then β 7→ Z β would be a nonzero linear functional invariant
under StabG (Z), again a contradiction to Lem. 6.3.
   Therefore dim Z = 2, and by Lemma 6.4 we have σ|Zreg = 0. For i = 1, 2,
v ∈ Tx Z and λ ∈ Tf∗i (x) P2 , by (3.3) and (6.8) we have
                       λ(dfi,x (v)) = σx (Ai,x (λ), v) = 0.
Hence both f1 and f2 are constant on Z. This contradicts the finiteness of
(f1 , f2 ) proved in Lem. 6.2.
   Every P-orbit therefore meets U , and we conclude by Prop. 3.6.      □
   As our fourfold X was constructed by choosing a Baire generic parameter
t (see the end of § 6.1), we proved:
Corollary 6.6. There are infinitely many Oka projective hyperkähler man-
ifolds.
